coherence.reasons: Both run a clean line from governing thought to executive summary to action titles to decisions. X's hierarchy is more explicit: seven conditions tested against the CEO's hypothesis, numbered sections matching the summary, and gates that deliver the 'hard gates' promise. But X has small internal inconsistencies. It says the worst tested case costs $6.4M ('about a third of the cap') while its own slide 13 shows -$7.5M at 38% ACoS with 25% duty. Its margin floor is stated as 9.0% in one place and 8.8% in another. Its slide 4 title ('$40M would need only about 1%') sits awkwardly with the later finding that no route reaches $40M. Y's one-page scorecard against the board's five tests is tidy and its numbers are consistent throughout ($7.5M and 8.7% in the worst case). Y's weaker points are a topical decisions title and leading on planning-case inputs while calling payback 'likely'. These roughly offset.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the same defensible recommendation: Amazon-led with gates, retail only above 20% awareness, ambition re-phased to about 2032, Japan deferred to 2028. Both weigh Japan fairly; Y's framing (give up about $19M of revenue to avoid about $4M of downside) is especially crisp. X goes further on what would trigger a change. Gate 1 and Gate 2 have explicit thresholds and if-missed actions, including scale-back or exit, with the loss quantified at about $2.4M to $3.7M. X also models a stall case from the two Amazon-first peers that stayed below $5M. It gives the board an explicit choice between re-phasing the ambition and relaxing the guardrails, and notes that Option A's plan is not conservative against Saebom. Y's guardrails are softer (slow growth and re-forecast, board review beyond the envelope) and it calls payback 'likely' when break-even ACoS is 28.6% against a pilot of 28% and a benchmark of 32%.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key numbers: unit contributions of $10.73, $4.01 and $7.55; Option B peak of -$20.8M and 4.5% margin; Option A at +2.4, +0.4 and -2.3; break-even ACoS of 28.6% (26.9% with the tariff); and the $5.2B correction. Both test the 4.5 units per door and 25% ACoS assumptions against the benchmarks. X uses the evidence more deeply: it puts the 28% and 32% cases and an evidence-based Option B case in the headline comparison, and adds a sell-through by halo grid, stall, volume and FX cases, and a model of the 2029 retail step. But X brushes two traps. Its slide 4 title uses 1%-share market sizing, and it extrapolates the pilot trend linearly to 333k units to support the 2027 plan. It also understates its own worst case ($6.4M against -$7.5M on its chart). Y is cleaner on the traps: it uses the June run-rate of 168k and says later years are untested, and its critique of the 0.71 correlation is fuller (common cause, reverse causation, no before-and-after, survey). Y's slips are an unsupported title claim that Amazon-first brands 'lost far less' (the pack gives no losses for them) and a scorecard built on planning inputs. Depth favours X and cleanliness favours Y.

revision.reasons: Both keep the CEO's hypothesis with conditions, as the evidence supports: Amazon first, with the retail trigger raised from 15% to 20% awareness, extra gates added, and the $40M date reset. X handles it more rigorously. It breaks the hypothesis into seven testable conditions with a verdict on each (holds, at risk, fails). It also models the CEO's 2029 national-retail step, showing group margin falling to 6.0% and cumulative cash to -$13.8M even at 4.6 units per door, so the retail leg fails on the guardrails as well as on awareness. Y's side-by-side table of the CEO's gates against proposed gates is clear and well reasoned, including repeat and ACoS-qualified sales gates. But its case against the 2029 step is mostly qualitative ('would break payback').

overall.reasons: The two documents reach the same sound recommendation on essentially the same model outputs, and both meet all four defensibility criteria. Y is tighter, numerically consistent and avoids the market-sizing and trend-extrapolation slips. X gives the board more to act on: evidence-based cases in the headline comparison, explicit gates with exit and scale-back triggers and quantified loss caps, a stall scenario grounded in the two stalled peers, a quantified test of the CEO's 2029 retail step, and a clear choice on ambition against guardrails. X's slips (the 1%-share title, the 333k extrapolation, the $6.4M against $7.5M worst case) are minor and do not affect the conclusion. X serves the decision maker slightly better.
